newsitem.title: DENMARK: NATO ministers tell candidates to be patient.
newsitem.headline: NATO ministers tell candidates to be patient.

text.p: NATO defence ministers sought to encourage the former Soviet Baltic republics in their bid for membership on Tuesday, while reassuring Russia that an enlarged alliance was no threat.

In a speech prepared for delivery to a closed-door seminar on Baltic Sea regional security attended by NATO, ex-Warsaw Pact and non-aligned officials, German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said eastern European countries not immediately able to join NATO must not feel rejected.
"Neither NATO nor the European Union can take in all countries who wish to become members at the same time. But the door will remain open to those who cannot join with the first wave," he said.

Although a firm decision on new members is not expected before a NATO summit early next year, Hungary, Poland the Czech Republic and Slovakia are widely seen as the most immediate candidates, with the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, along with Bulgaria and Romania, joining later.

The Baltic republics, which broke away from the Soviet Union amid bloodshed in 1991, are already actively involved in Western defence structures, participating in a Danish-led Nordic peacekeeping brigade in Bosnia.

They are to take part in Baltic Circle 1996, a multinational military exercise within the framework of NATO's Partnership for Peace (PfP) programme ,taking place in Denmark from September 30 to October 11.
A Baltic peacekeeping battalion is being trained in Nordic countries and British Defence Minister Michael Portillo told the seminar his country would extend its training programme next year.
While the Baltic states and other former Soviet republics and satellites are nervous of their huge and volatile Russian neighbour, Moscow is uneasy about NATO expanding on its borders.
At the moment Norway is the only alliance member with a land frontier with Russia.

The United States, represented at the seminar by Defence Secretary William Perry, and other NATO members have taken pains to assuage Russian anxiety, suggesting that Moscow could join a future, intensified, version of PfP.
Portillo and Ruehe both said current and planned NATO reforms meant the alliance was no longer the adversary force it had been during the Cold War.
Ruehe said NATO's new priorities were cooperation, crisis management and encouraging stability.
"NATO enlargement is not a matter of expanding outdated military structures to the East or widening zones of influence."
"What NATO enlargement is all about is opening an alliance to independent, democratic, sovereign European countries, committed to democracy, the market economy and shared values."
Also taking part in the Copenhagen seminar, hosted by Danish Defence Minister Hans Haekkerup, are his counterparts from Sweden, the Netherlands and the three Baltic states.
Russia is represented by a Russia-North America think-tank while Poland and Norway have sent senior defence officals.
No decisions were to be taken in Copenhagen.

But views could emerge that Perry and NATO defence ministers will be able to pass on to their Russian counterpart Igor Rodionov when they meet him at a separate conference in Norway on Wednesday and Thursday.
